title: The Unchanging Essence and the Names of the Trinity
english: And indeed the whole sense of these words leans toward his becoming man. For when he said, “I am the Son of God,” and they retorted, “You blaspheme” (John 10:36), the Father ratified it for him: “This alone is my true Son.” That is what “this,” and “beloved,” and his being named “Son” with the article make plain. “In this one,” he says, “I was well pleased that through his becoming man salvation should be won for you.”

And even if someone takes “I was well pleased” of his Godhead, their sophism is made void. For not every expression spoken by God, and least of all about God the Word, yields a meaning by the custom of this world. Then again, if he said “in whom I was well pleased” of the Son who already existed, the good pleasure is not found to be the cause of his existence.

To make plainer what such an expression signifies, let us take as our witness the one who sings in Psalm 149, “For the Lord takes pleasure in his people” (Psalm 149:4). The good pleasure did not come about before the people, but after them. For he took pleasure in them, and sent them peace and grace, at the times when they served him rightly. When they did not, the reverse, as he now prophesies: “When he slew them, then they sought him” (Psalm 78:34). And in Psalm 44: “Their arm did not save them, but your right hand, and your arm, and the light of your face, because you took pleasure in them” (Psalm 44:3). Here he names the Son “the right hand and arm of God” and “the light of his face.” And in Psalm 106: “Remember us, Lord, in the good pleasure of your people” (Psalm 106:4).
On their saying, “If the unbegotten God is wholly generative, he did not beget from his essence,” and, “If his essence was changed into an offspring, the essence of God is not unchangeable.”

This too is theirs, a random and faulty argument, set down in words like these: “If the unbegotten God is wholly generative, the one begotten was not begotten from his essence, since his whole essence has the property of begetting, but not of being begotten.”

But let them hear this: “If the light is wholly generative, it does not beget its radiance from its essence but takes it on from outside, since its whole essence has the property of begetting, but not of being begotten.” But if the light does not take on its radiance from outside, but begets it from its whole essence without any interval, then neither did God acquire the Son from outside. He begot him from his whole hypostasis without any interval, since he is without body. That is why he is truly Father.

Again they press on, everywhere pursuing a course contrary to Scripture: “If the essence of God, by being transformed, is called offspring, then his essence is not unchangeable, since it was the change that brought about the Son’s own distinct being.”

But no one grants them leave to say even this. For the Scripture we have mentioned proves such talk foreign to Christians, and it stands against every heretical and most grievous disorder. For if light, by being transformed, becomes radiance, then light is not unchangeable, since the change brings about the radiance’s own distinct being. But if light has begotten radiance without being changed, remaining light itself and having from itself its radiance, complete and grown together with it, then God too remains God without turning, being Father of his own radiance. He did not take it on from outside, but begot it complete from his essence.
On those who prattle that, on the ground of the name “Father,” the essence of the Son himself is different.

Going round and round the same things on the same subjects, and counterfeiting the beauty of the truth at every point, they say this too, without love for God: things whose names differ must also differ in essence. For he says, “The word ‘Father’ does not signify the word ‘Son,’ nor does the name ‘Son’ show the hypostasis of the Father.”

But let them hear, first, this. If the divine hypostases had not been made known by fitting names, what sign could anyone have used to make known the Father himself, and that he has a Son, without saying the name “Father”? Or how, without naming the names “Son” and “Spirit,” could anyone have addressed the Son himself or the Spirit, and shown that the Son has a Father and that the Spirit is the Spirit of God?

And second, this. In the holy Trinity, apart from the one who truly is Father being called Father, and the one who was begotten by nature being called Only-begotten, and the one who is exactly what it has been called, and belongs to the Father, being named Spirit of God, all the other names stand the same: such as God, Lord, holy, righteous, good, light, life. title: The Son Without Beginning, from John’s Prologue
english: … same, their essence too stands as one, so that it follows that like is marked out by like. For to the true and eternal light, in relation to the true and eternal light, and to the truly [...]

“I am God, and there is no other besides me. There is no righteous one and Saviour except me. Turn to me and you will be saved, you who are from the end of the earth. I am God, and there is no other. By myself I swear: righteousness shall surely go out of my mouth, and my words shall not be turned back, that to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall swear by God” (Isaiah 45:21-23), which means, will acknowledge God, or “will confess to God.”

So God the Father is not ahead of the Son, not in being without beginning, not in essence, not in glory. They stand on equal terms, except perhaps in the matter of fatherhood. For that these are the words of the only-begotten Son the inspired Paul made clear when he wrote to the Romans, saying: “For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, as it is written: As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God” (Romans 14:10-11).

Likewise John the theologian too said in the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being that has come into being. In him was life, and the life was the light of men. And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not grasp it” (John 1:1-5). And in the Revelation: “He who is and who was and who is to come, the Lord our God, the Almighty” (Revelation 1:8).

“He who is” signifies the everlasting being of the divine hypostasis, as we have said elsewhere too. For the expression is without limit, and that is why God gave “He who is” as his own name (Exodus 3:14).

“In the beginning was” (John 1:1) sets in plain view, and makes very clear indeed, how absurd and how much to be shunned is the saying “There was when he was not.” For the word “was” is indefinite. In Latin this indefinite form is made up of two words, the “pluperfect,” which is rendered “more than perfect.” So here it requires that he be understood as beyond time altogether, or without beginning. For if anyone were to say that he was not in the beginning, then the beginning, which has no cause, would once not have been. And again, how can time, which did not yet exist, be the measure of the one who made it?

“Was with God” (John 1:1) sets before us the kinship of nature that the Son has with God the Father, and that from the time the self-originate Father was (if it is lawful to say so) the Son who is from him exists together with him. “Was with God” could also be understood in a strong sense: that like God he was without beginning, unoriginate, uncontainable, good, immortal, King of all. For if this were not so with the wisdom that has welled up, it would not be so with the spring that sent the wisdom welling up either. But it is so with both. For John’s aim, and his word handed down from God, is clear, firm, free of idle subtlety, and looks to the divine alone.
“The Word was God” (John 1:1) establishes that the Word has real being, and that he is God such as that God is whose Word he is; and again, that he has no cause.

“All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being” (John 1:3) shows him, as has been said already, to be not only Creator, but also not created. For if not one created thing received its being without him, it is plain to everyone that he himself did not come into being, but was begotten as God is begotten. Indeed, it is impossible that he who gave existence to the universe, and essence and immortality to rational beings, should have come from non-being into being. For nothing created can give essence, or immortality, or make beings rational. It works only on the substance of gold, or silver, or bronze, or iron, or wood, or stone, already brought out of non-being by God, and from it fashions something without soul or reason, a statue perhaps, or something else. But this very thing, to bring forth an essence that was not, or to show it forth as living and rational, is the peculiar and singular property of the one all-powerful and self-complete divine nature alone. And the Father made all things through him as light makes through its own radiance, and as mind through word.

“In him was life” (John 1:4) teaches us further that he is without beginning, being the life of the one supreme nature, and that when nothing at all existed he was the cause of the things that exist. That is why he himself says, “I am the life” (John 14:6), “I am the light” (John 8:12).

He is lavish with testimonies to the one without beginning, saying “was” so many times, so that by repeating such a word he might either open the deaf ears of heretics, or leave no pretext at all for “There was when he was not” at the coming universal and unswerving judgment.
“And the life was the light of men” (John 1:4) teaches the same things once more. For he says: this …

title: The Son Is Called the Almighty
english: … unoriginate life is what holds together the originate nature of human beings.

“And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not grasp it” (John 1:5) does not tolerate the opinions of the heretics. For it shows, not obscurely but with great sharpness, that whatever time before time, or briefest instant, or age before the ages anyone may suppose, he shines eternally as the inseparable radiance of God, and the darkness of non-existence never grasped it.

“The Almighty” (Revelation 1:8) needs no interpretation at all. For it shows that he holds the kingdom undivided with God the Father and his Holy Spirit, and that he is “God over all” (Romans 9:5). “Who is to come” (Revelation 1:8) shows the Son, who is going to come a second time and “judge the living and the dead” (2 Timothy 4:1).

So John the Baptist too, establishing that “He who is” was said of the Son, makes it plain when he says to the Master, “Are you” (that is, are you that One who is, whom, when you were God in the womb of the Virgin, I myself, being in the belly of the barren woman, recognized and worshipped by my leaping), “or do we look for another?” (Matthew 11:3).

And John, the friend and apostle of the Lord, writes in his first epistle as well: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life (and the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and bear witness, and declare to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us), that which we have seen and heard we declare to you also, so that you too may have fellowship with us. And our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ” (1 John 1:1-3).

Mark once more how often he says “was,” and how those who do not confess that he is Son by nature, without beginning together with God, have no fellowship of salvation with the Father or with the Only-begotten. For it is in this faith, handed down to us by the Master of all in the mystery-teaching of the illumination, that we have the fellowship of which Peter wrote, “that you may become partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4). For a creature, a thing subject to time, is not divine nature.
Remember besides that he said “our fellowship” is “with the Father and with his Son,” with equal honour, and not “through his Son.”

And Amos too, in his prophecy, likewise names the Son “Almighty,” saying somewhere like this: “He who builds his ascent into heaven, and lays the foundation of his promise upon the earth; who calls the water of the sea and pours it out upon the face of all the earth: the Lord God Almighty is his name” (Amos 9:6). Of this ascent David too sings: “God went up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet” (Psalm 47:5).

Both these sayings are about the Son. For the Father neither came down nor went up, as the Apostle explains when he writes: “Now what does ‘he went up’ mean, if not that he also first came down? He who came down is the very one who also went up far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” (Ephesians 4:9-10). He means: as one who has risen above all things and surpasses them, together with the Father who begot him, since he is unoriginate. For it is plain that he understood it so, from the fact that the spiritual powers, too, since they are measured creatures, are in heaven, but not above the heavens, and do not fill all things.

And Zephaniah likewise proclaims him “Almighty,” saying: “This shall be theirs in return for their insolence, because they reproached and magnified themselves against the Lord Almighty. The Lord will appear against them, and the Lord will utterly destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth, and they will worship him, each from his own place” (Zephaniah 2:10-11).

And Malachi, following on, says in the person of the Master: “For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice; for my name is great among the nations, says the Lord Almighty. But you profane it” (Malachi 1:11-12).

For the mention both of his appearing and of his being glorified among the nations shows that the Son is meant, whose name the Jews profane together with those who worship a creature. And the very sequence of the text requires him to be Almighty, since, as image and only-begotten of the Almighty, he must be understood as image of the Almighty in this too.

And Paul writes to the Hebrews: “who, being the radiance of the glory of the Father” (Hebrews 1:3), that is, without beginning together with him and of one essence with him. For so that things beyond comparison might be shown somehow by a comparison, if even so what is beyond the mind might be taken into the mind in some measure, …
